overview: The British Raj was Crown rule in the Indian subcontinent from 1858 to 1947. The map covers only 1878 to 1938. Its outline mixes political authorities and includes Burma across changes in status, as explained below.

periods.title: Crown government
periods.summary: British Crown rule began in 1858. A viceroy, governors and appointed councils exercised colonial authority.

periods.title: Organized political demands
periods.summary: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885. Limited council reforms did not give the wider population control over government.

periods.title: War and mass resistance
periods.summary: Indian soldiers served overseas during the First World War. Amritsar in 1919 and the Salt Satyagraha of 1930 became defining episodes of the struggle against colonial rule.

periods.title: War, hunger and departure
periods.summary: The Second World War period brought renewed demands for British withdrawal and catastrophic hunger in Bengal. In 1947, independence and Partition ended the Raj.

items.text: The viceroy and provincial governors governed through councils dominated by appointed officials. Indian participation expanded slowly, but early elected council members could advise without making the governor answerable to them. Holding a seat therefore did not mean sharing the power of an elected government.

Princely states had a different relationship to British power from directly administered provinces. A February 1947 policy draft explicitly distinguished Britain’s powers over the Indian states from the government of British India. The single colored outline hides these different political arrangements.

The map’s Burmese extension needs particular care. British forces invaded Upper Burma in 1885; annexation followed in 1886. Burma became separately administered in 1937. The imported outline already includes Upper Burma in 1878 and still includes Burma after separation, so those edges should not be treated as reliable borders for each year.

The Congress organization created in 1885 became an important forum for Indian political demands. Indians also disagreed about empire: Dadabhai Naoroji criticized British rule, while another Indian MP in London, M. M. Bhownaggree, supported the Raj. Shared origins did not produce identical political opinions.

On 13 April 1919, troops fired on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, killing hundreds. The exact total remains disputed. The massacre deeply damaged trust in British government and strengthened the independence movement. This was a turning point in relations between rulers and ruled.

In March 1930, Gandhi told the viceroy in advance that he intended to break the salt law. He announced a march to Dandi, then left Sabarmati Ashram with followers on 12 March. An ordinary substance used in food became the focus of a carefully announced challenge to colonial authority.

Imported factory cloth put intense pressure on Indian spinning and weaving. The V&A describes unemployment and hardship as Lancashire goods displaced much handmade production. A piece of fabric could carry a long chain of work behind it: growers, spinners, weavers and sellers all depended on what customers bought.

Gandhi urged people to spin, weave and wear khadi, cloth made from hand-spun thread. The spinning wheel appeared on a nationalist flag in 1921. Surviving Gujarat khadi dated about 1867 also reminds us that the material preceded that campaign. Political protest could begin with the clothes in someone’s cupboard.

Gandhi’s 1917 railway account describes a Bombay-to-Madras carriage labeled for 22 passengers that held as many as 35. Travelers spent two nights without sleeping bunks; some stood or slept on a dirty floor. Railways connected distant places, but a ticket could buy a very uncomfortable journey.

The same account says the carriage toilet went uncleaned and its water tank was empty. Gandhi asked senior officials to try third-class travel without warning the railway first. His proposed inspection had a practical sting: if important passengers needed water and a clean seat, so did everyone else.

Anandibai Joshee, born in 1865, married as a child and later lost an infant. She described the need for better medical care as a reason to study medicine. In 1886 she graduated from Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania. Her story connects family experience with a determined effort to open a professional path for women.

Studying abroad also meant negotiating food and clothing. Joshee continued wearing a sari to classes, and the college dean housed her so she could obtain familiar food. She accepted a hospital post caring for women in Kolhapur, but died in 1887 before beginning practice. Her college preserved correspondence and course records.

Rabindranath Tagore founded a residential school at Santiniketan in 1901. Its learning included nature, music and art, with classrooms outdoors beneath trees. A university followed in 1921. Imagine looking up from a lesson and finding leaves overhead: the setting was part of an educational vision linking Indian traditions with human fellowship across cultural boundaries.

In a 1928 scientific letter from Calcutta, C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan reported experiments on light scattered by dust-free liquids and gases. Alongside light of the original frequency, they detected a changed component. Tiny differences in scattered light could reveal behavior of molecules too small to watch directly.

A Gujarati writing sample is “હિન્દ સ્વરાજ”, the title Hind Swaraj, translated as “Indian Home Rule”. Gandhi wrote the work in 1909 and translated it into English in 1910. The Gujarati spelling here comes from a modern digital edition. It preserves one influential Indian voice in a society with many languages and scripts.

The Raj drew Indian people into distant wars. In Mesopotamia in October 1918, medical officer Heerajee Cursetjee and fellow medics treated and evacuated wounded men under fire. His medal citation recorded exhausting work across two days. Armies depended on medical skill and care as well as weapons; Indian service helped sustain Britain’s global military power.

By August 1943, an American diplomatic report described starving villagers arriving in Calcutta and dying there. It recorded an appeal for hospitals to admit people who had collapsed and urged rice shipments if transport could be found. These documents show officials receiving urgent warnings during Bengal’s famine, while food and care failed to reach many families.

In July 1942, Jawaharlal Nehru explained that the demand for independence required British withdrawal. He proposed a provisional government representing major groups, including Congress and the Muslim League. Such proposals show that anti-colonial politics also involved a difficult question: how would different political communities govern together after Britain left?

Independence in August 1947 came with Partition into India and Pakistan. Millions crossed new borders, while violence devastated many communities. A contemporary officer’s account recorded Indian soldiers desperately worrying about relatives in Punjab. Political independence and family catastrophe could occur at the same time; both belong in this history.

ending.text: Crown rule ended in August 1947 with independent India and Pakistan. The map’s 1938 cutoff is not the Raj’s ending. Communities, languages and cultural institutions continued through Partition’s upheaval.
